These tones are pertinent in the language and the evidence for considering them as such will be given under the section 'Phonemic tone Contrast'. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Esimbi is described as a tone language with five lexical tones (high, mid, low, falling, rising); the only suprasegmental features treated are vowel length and tone. The thesis makes no statement about word stress or accent at all, so no stress position can be read from it.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: few minimal pairs by tone alone because words are multisyllabic; verbs (imperative) carry only H/L patterns (H or LH on monosyllables; HH/LH on disyllables; HHH/LLH/LHH on trisyllables); noun prefixes mostly L or H, exceptionally M/HL/LH.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical tone on words in isolation; verbs cited in imperative form). No phrase-level prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Fointein 1986 describes Esimbi as spoken in the Benakuma area (Menchum Division, NW Cameroon); no dialect is singled out and the description is for the language as a whole (esim1238). Kalinowski 2009 likewise centres on Benakuma. No differently named variety is involved.

Chapter 5 'Suprasegmental phonology' (pp. 73-80) treats only vowel length and tone: Esimbi is called a tone language with five tones (H, M, L, HL falling, LH rising); the words 'stress', 'accent', 'prominence' do not occur anywhere in the scanned text and chapter 5 was read in full (page images pp. 73-74 checked).
Segment inventory only, sourced from Fointein 1986; no tones or stress listed.

sources.note: Says nothing about word stress or about whether Esimbi is tonal beyond the aside 'tones are omitted'; it neither supports nor contradicts the existing Fointein 1986 statement (tone language, five tones, no stress statement). Its Esimbi data are second-hand from Hyman 1988 and Stallcup 1980.
